synopsis: Structure from motion recovers camera positions and 3D points from photographs; COLMAP implements this method, while scene reconstruction extends it into a usable virtual site through registration, cleanup, classification, collision proxies, sensor materials and qualification against held-out measurements [f13144, f13145, f13151]. The booklet calls existing machine recordings the cheapest route to real site geometry, but reconstruction requires synchronized, calibrated logs and accurate poses; in one dataset, only 50 of 200 sequences passed the pose check [f13153, f4216, f4290, f13152]. Camera-only reconstruction depends on texture, similar illumination, overlap, at least three observations per object and genuinely different viewpoints; textureless terrain, glare, reflective surfaces and insufficient parallax can cause failure [f3799, f4034, f4035, f4040]. One benchmark required more than 800 hours of COLMAP compute and more than 300 hours of manual selection, but the compute figure is on-road evidence, not a direct job-site digital-twin cost estimate [f13150, f3898]. The conclusion is that reconstruction can make recordings replay-ready or near-path simulation-ready, but not braking-validation-ready or radar/ultrasonic-ready: reconstructed mesh artifacts actually occluded simulated radar and produced empty frames, so sensor-mounting comparisons require validated reconstruction and position-specific sensor models [f13154, f5103, f5492].
